ADULT ADOPTION IN CALIFORNIA — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Morgan T. Ellis

DECLARATION OF PURPOSE — ADULT ADOPTION INFORMATION SHEET
This Adult Adoption — Information Sheet describes California's statutory process, set out in Family Code Division 13, Part 3, Chapter 2 (Procedure for Adult Adoption, §§ 9320-9328), for Jordan Lee to adopt Morgan T. Ellis, an adult. It is prepared for use alongside an actual adult-adoption petition contemplated for filing in the California superior court for Sacramento County.

Adult adoption is a legally separate track from every minor-adoption process this corpus otherwise documents. This corpus's Stepparent Adoption — Information Sheet (Family Code Chapter 5, §§ 9000-9007) and Independent Adoption — Information Sheet (Family Code Chapter 3, §§ 8800-8823) both govern the adoption of a child under 18, built around a birth parent's or existing legal parent's consent, and this corpus's Guardianship of the Person (Petition Information Sheet) governs custody of a minor without creating any new parent-child relationship at all. Adult adoption instead begins from a written agreement between two adults — the prospective adoptive parent and the person proposed to be adopted, who must already be 18 or older — that both of them sign, and it does not involve a birth parent's consent to the adoption at all. This document's companion clauses describe who may enter that agreement, what a petition for its approval must contain, the hearing and appearance requirements, when an investigation is and is not required, a narrower notice requirement specific to adoptions of adults with developmental disabilities, the court's approval standard, and the adoption's effect on inheritance from the adoptee's birth family.

This information sheet is not itself a court filing. Completing it does not adopt Morgan T. Ellis, does not affect any person's inheritance rights, and does not determine that any specific adoption should or will be granted. Only a final court order of adoption, entered after the statutory petition, hearing, and approval process described in this document's companion clauses, can actually do that.

WHO MAY ADOPT WHOM, AND THE WRITTEN ADOPTION AGREEMENT
Family Code § 9320(a) provides that "An adult may adopt another adult who is younger, except the spouse of the prospective adoptive parent, by an adoption agreement approved by the court, as provided in this chapter." Two eligibility limits appear in that single sentence: the proposed adoptee must be younger than Jordan Lee, and Jordan Lee may not adopt a current spouse. Unlike the minor-adoption processes this corpus separately documents, in which a birth parent or existing legal parent consents to the child's adoption by someone else, an adult adoption under this chapter rests on the adoptee's own act, not a third party's consent on the adoptee's behalf. Family Code § 9320(b) states this directly: "The adoption agreement shall be in writing, executed by the prospective adoptive parent and the proposed adoptee, and shall state that the parties agree to assume toward each other the legal relationship of parent and child and to have all of the rights and be subject to all of the duties and responsibilities of that relationship." That jointly executed written agreement — not a separate one-sided consent form signed only by Morgan T. Ellis — is the mechanism by which Morgan T. Ellis's agreement to the adoption is expressed under this chapter.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "An adult may adopt another adult who is younger, except the spouse of the prospective adoptive parent, by an adoption agreement approved by the court, as provided in this chapter."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9320(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9320(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9320.)
  "The adoption agreement shall be in writing, executed by the prospective adoptive parent and the proposed adoptee, and shall state that the parties agree to assume toward each other the legal relationship of parent and child and to have all of the rights and be subject to all of the duties and responsibilities of that relationship."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9320(b) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9320(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9320.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own eligibility rule and its own written-agreement mechanism for adult adoption — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular adult adoption, and not a claim that any specific adoption agreement between the prospective adoptive parent and the proposed adoptee named in this document has been, or will be, approved. § 9320(a) and § 9320(b) are subsections of the same statutory section and are treated as one source. This clause corrects one assumption sometimes made about this process: this chapter's own text does not require a separate written consent document signed only by the adoptee, and it does not require the consent of the adoptee's spouse (if any) to the adoption at all — the only spouse this chapter's eligibility rule mentions is the prospective adoptive parent's own spouse, whom the prospective adoptive parent may not adopt. This clause does not address whether a court could decline to approve a specific adoption agreement on other, case-specific grounds; that determination is addressed by this document's companion clause on the court's approval standard at the hearing.

THE PETITION FOR APPROVAL OF THE ADOPTION AGREEMENT
Family Code § 9321(a) provides that "The prospective adoptive parent and the proposed adoptee may file in the county in which either person resides a petition for approval of the adoption agreement" — meaning venue for Jordan Lee and Morgan T. Ellis's petition may rest on either person's residence in Sacramento County, not only Jordan Lee's. Family Code § 9321(b) then lists six specific items the petition must state, including "The length and nature of the relationship between the prospective adoptive parent and the proposed adoptee," "The degree of kinship, if any," "The reason the adoption is sought," "A statement as to why the adoption would be in the best interest of the prospective adoptive parent, the proposed adoptee, and the public," the names and addresses of the proposed adoptee's living birth parents or adult children, if any, and "[w]hether the prospective adoptive parent or the prospective adoptive parent's spouse has previously adopted any other adult and, if so, the name of the adult, together with the date and place of the adoption."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The prospective adoptive parent and the proposed adoptee may file in the county in which either person resides a petition for approval of the adoption agreement."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9321(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9321(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9321.)
  "Whether the prospective adoptive parent or the prospective adoptive parent’s spouse has previously adopted any other adult and, if so, the name of the adult, together with the date and place of the adoption."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9321(b) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9321(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9321.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own venue rule and its own required petition content for adult adoption — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular adult adoption, and not a claim that any specific petition by the prospective adoptive parent and proposed adoptee named in this document states or omits any of these six items. § 9321(a) and § 9321(b) are subsections of the same statutory section and are treated as one source. This clause quotes four of the six numbered items in § 9321(b) verbatim and paraphrases the remaining two (the degree-of-kinship item and the living-birth-parents/adult-children item) only to the extent needed to introduce the sixth quoted item in context; it does not restate every procedural detail a specific superior court's local rules or forms may additionally require for filing. This document does not itself state, and does not verify, the length or nature of any relationship, the degree of kinship, or the reason for the adoption described in a specific petition.

SETTING THE HEARING, NOTICE TO INTERESTED PERSONS, AND PERSONAL APPEARANCE
Once Jordan Lee and Morgan T. Ellis file their petition, Family Code § 9322 requires that "[w]hen the petition for approval of the adoption agreement is filed, the court clerk shall set the matter for hearing." Family Code § 9323 then allows the court to bring in others who may have an interest in the outcome: "The court may require notice of the time and place of the hearing to be served on any other interested person and any interested person may appear and object to the proposed adoption." At the hearing itself, Family Code § 9324 requires personal presence rather than representation by counsel alone, subject to one cross-referenced exception: "Both the prospective adoptive parent and the proposed adoptee shall appear at the hearing in person, unless the court allows otherwise pursuant to Section 8613.5."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "When the petition for approval of the adoption agreement is filed, the court clerk shall set the matter for hearing."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9322 (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9322 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9322.)
  "The court may require notice of the time and place of the hearing to be served on any other interested person and any interested person may appear and object to the proposed adoption."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9323 (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9323 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9323.)
  "Both the prospective adoptive parent and the proposed adoptee shall appear at the hearing in person, unless the court allows otherwise pursuant to Section 8613.5."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9324 (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9324 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9324.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own hearing-setting, notice, and appearance rules for adult adoption — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular adult adoption, and not a claim that any specific hearing has been, or will be, set for the petition described in this document. §§ 9322, 9323, and 9324 are three separate, independently numbered sections and are treated as three independent sources. This clause does not itself state the content of § 8613.5 (remote appearance), which is quoted here only by cross-reference within § 9324's own text; this clause does not independently verify § 8613.5's substantive remote-appearance criteria. This session's one lightweight CourtListener check for California appellate decisions construing "interested person" under § 9323, or the personal-appearance requirement under § 9324, returned a 429 daily-quota-exceeded error (125 requests/day) before any case could be retrieved, so this clause is statute-text-only and does not report how courts have applied either provision on specific facts. Family Code § 9324 was last amended in 2022 (effective January 1, 2023); this clause reports its current text as fetched from the state's own legislative information website on the date above, not an earlier or later version.

NO GENERAL INVESTIGATION REQUIREMENT, AND A NARROWER NOTICE REQUIREMENT FOR ADULTS WITH DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
Family Code § 9325 states the general rule for adult adoption: "No investigation or report to the court by any public officer or agency is required, but the court may require the county probation officer or the department to investigate the circumstances of the proposed adoption and report thereon, with recommendations, to the court before the hearing." That default — no mandatory home study or investigation, with the court retaining discretion to order one — does not apply without exception. Family Code § 9326 requires Jordan Lee to give specific additional notice "in any case in which both of the following conditions exist: (a) The proposed adoptee is an adult with developmental disabilities. (b) The prospective adoptive parent is a provider of board and care, treatment, habilitation, or other services to persons with developmental disabilities or is a spouse or employee of a provider," including notice to "the director of the regional center for the developmentally disabled" at least 30 days before the hearing. Where Jordan Lee is such a provider (or that provider's spouse or employee) and seeks to adopt an unrelated adult with developmental disabilities, Family Code § 9327 requires that regional center to "file a written report with the court regarding the suitability of the proposed adoption in meeting the needs of the proposed adoptee and regarding any known previous adoption by the prospective adoptive parent."

  "(a) The proposed adoptee is an adult with developmental disabilities. (b) The prospective adoptive parent is a provider of board and care, treatment, habilitation, or other services to persons with developmental disabilities or is a spouse or employee of a provider."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9326 (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9326 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9326.)
  "file a written report with the court regarding the suitability of the proposed adoption in meeting the needs of the proposed adoptee and regarding any known previous adoption by the prospective adoptive parent."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9327 (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9327 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9327.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own default investigation rule and its own narrower exception for adults with developmental disabilities adopted by their care providers — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular adult adoption, and not a claim that the proposed adoptee named in this document is or is not an adult with developmental disabilities, or that the prospective adoptive parent named in this document is or is not a provider within the meaning of these sections. §§ 9325, 9326, and 9327 are three separate, independently numbered sections and are treated as three independent sources; the § 9326(a)-(b) quotation is drawn from that one section's own subdivisions. This clause paraphrases § 9326's cross-reference to the Welfare and Institutions Code defining a regional center, and does not independently verify that cross-referenced Welfare and Institutions Code text. This clause does not restate every procedural detail of how or on whom notice under § 9326 must be served beyond the regional center director and the proposed adoptee's living birth parents or adult children, and it does not determine whether the conditions triggering §§ 9326-9327 are met in any specific case.

THE COURT'S APPROVAL STANDARD AT THE HEARING
Family Code § 9328(a) requires the court itself to question the parties at the hearing: "At the hearing the court shall examine the parties, or the counsel of any party not present in person." § 9328(b) then sets the standard for approval or denial: "If the court is satisfied that the adoption will be in the best interests of the persons seeking the adoption and in the public interest and that there is no reason why the petition should not be granted, the court shall approve the adoption agreement and make an order of adoption declaring that the person adopted is the child of the adoptive parent. Otherwise, the court shall withhold approval of the agreement and deny the petition." § 9328(c) relaxes the ordinary evidentiary rules for that determination: "In determining whether or not the adoption of any person pursuant to this part is in the best interests of the persons seeking the adoption or the public interest, the court may consider evidence, oral or written, whether or not it is in conformity with the Evidence Code."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]

  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9328(a) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9328(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9328.)
  "If the court is satisfied that the adoption will be in the best interests of the persons seeking the adoption and in the public interest and that there is no reason why the petition should not be granted, the court shall approve the adoption agreement and make an order of adoption declaring that the person adopted is the child of the adoptive parent."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9328(b) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9328(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9328.)
  "In determining whether or not the adoption of any person pursuant to this part is in the best interests of the persons seeking the adoption or the public interest, the court may consider evidence, oral or written, whether or not it is in conformity with the Evidence Code."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 9328(c) (California Legislative Information text), Fam. C. § 9328(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=9328.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own approval standard for adult adoption — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular adult adoption, and not a claim that any specific petition described in this document will be approved or denied. § 9328(a), (b), and (c) are subsections of the same statutory section and are treated as one source. This clause does not identify what would, in a specific case, constitute a reason the petition should not be granted; § 9328(b) leaves that determination to the court on the facts and evidence before it, admissible under § 9328(c)'s relaxed standard or not. This document does not itself examine the parties, weigh evidence, or make any best-interest determination — only the court conducting the hearing described in this document's companion clause on hearing notice and appearance can do that.

EFFECT ON INHERITANCE FROM THE ADOPTEE'S BIRTH FAMILY
Family Code Chapter 2 itself does not state how a completed adult adoption affects Morgan T. Ellis's inheritance rights from Morgan T. Ellis's birth family; that question is addressed by California's separate intestate-succession statute, Probate Code § 6450 and § 6451, which apply to "an adopted person" without distinguishing an adult adoptee from a minor one. Probate Code § 6450(b) provides that "[t]he relationship of parent and child exists between an adopted person and the person's adopting parent or parents" for intestate-succession purposes. Probate Code § 6451(a) then sets the default rule for the birth-family relationship: "An adoption severs the relationship of parent and child between an adopted person and a natural parent of the adopted person unless both of the following requirements are satisfied: (1) The natural parent and the adopted person lived together at any time as parent and child, or the natural parent was married to or cohabiting with the other natural parent at the time the person was conceived and died before the person's birth. (2) The adoption was by the spouse of either of the natural parents or after the death of either of the natural parents." Because an adult adoption under Family Code §§ 9320-9328 does not require the adoptive parent to be a spouse of Morgan T. Ellis's natural parent or to be adopting after a natural parent's death, this severance default, not its narrow exception, will typically govern an adult adoption completed under this chapter for intestate-succession purposes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The relationship of parent and child exists between an adopted person and the person’s adopting parent or parents."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6450(b) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 6450(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6450.)
  "An adoption severs the relationship of parent and child between an adopted person and a natural parent of the adopted person unless both of the following requirements are satisfied: (1) The natural parent and the adopted person lived together at any time as parent and child, or the natural parent was married to or cohabiting with the other natural parent at the time the person was conceived and died before the person’s birth. (2) The adoption was by the spouse of either of the natural parents or after the death of either of the natural parents."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 6451(a) (California Legislative Information text), Prob. C. § 6451(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=6451.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of California's own default inheritance-severance rule for adopted persons generally, and of that rule's own narrow exception — not a claim about which state's law governs a particular estate, and not a claim that the proposed adoptee's specific circumstances do or do not satisfy Probate Code § 6451(a)'s exception. Probate Code § 6450 and § 6451 are separate, independently numbered sections and are treated as two independent sources; § 6450(a) (concerning natural parents generally) and § 6451(b)-(c) (concerning who inherits from or through the adopted person, and prior adoptive relationships) are not quoted or independently verified here. This clause corrects one assumption sometimes made about this topic: Probate Code §§ 6450-6451 do not contain a rule written specifically for adult adoption, or a rule that differs in its own terms from the rule that applies to the adoption of a minor; both draw on the same statutory text. This clause addresses only intestate succession — inheritance in the absence of a valid will — and does not address testate succession under a will, nonprobate transfers, or any other body of law that may treat an adopted adult differently for other purposes. This document does not itself determine the proposed adoptee's inheritance rights in any specific estate.

SIGNATURE AND ACKNOWLEDGMENT BLOCK — ADULT ADOPTION INFORMATION SHEET
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing background information is true and correct.

Executed on September 1, 2026 at Oakland, California.

Signature of Jordan Lee: ☐ _________________________

Signature of Morgan T. Ellis: ☐ _________________________

It does not itself constitute, replace, or complete that petition, and it does not adopt Morgan T. Ellis or affect any person's inheritance rights; only a final court order of adoption can do that.]

expectedJSON.body: Family Code Chapter 2 itself does not state how a completed adult adoption affects Morgan T. Ellis's inheritance rights from Morgan T. Ellis's birth family; that question is addressed by California's separate intestate-succession statute, Probate Code § 6450 and § 6451, which apply to "an adopted person" without distinguishing an adult adoptee from a minor one. Probate Code § 6450(b) provides that "[t]he relationship of parent and child exists between an adopted person and the person's adopting parent or parents" for intestate-succession purposes. Probate Code § 6451(a) then sets the default rule for the birth-family relationship: "An adoption severs the relationship of parent and child between an adopted person and a natural parent of the adopted person unless both of the following requirements are satisfied: (1) The natural parent and the adopted person lived together at any time as parent and child, or the natural parent was married to or cohabiting with the other natural parent at the time the person was conceived and died before the person's birth. (2) The adoption was by the spouse of either of the natural parents or after the death of either of the natural parents." Because an adult adoption under Family Code §§ 9320-9328 does not require the adoptive parent to be a spouse of Morgan T. Ellis's natural parent or to be adopting after a natural parent's death, this severance default, not its narrow exception, will typically govern an adult adoption completed under this chapter for intestate-succession purposes.
